title: Reliability Engineering
description: The principles and practices for running systems that meet explicit reliability targets at an acceptable cost.

sections.overview: Reliability engineering treats availability, latency and correctness as measurable product properties. It sets targets (SLOs), designs systems to meet them, measures them continuously, and learns from incidents.
sections.context: As systems become distributed, failures become partial and constant. Reliability engineering provides the tools to manage that: timeouts and retries with backoff, circuit breakers, redundancy, load shedding, graceful degradation, disaster recovery and blameless postmortems.
application: Define SLOs for user-facing journeys and use error budgets to balance features and stability.
Design for failure: every remote call has a timeout and a failure behaviour.
Practise recovery with game days and chaos experiments.
Write postmortems that lead to systemic fixes.
examples: The OpsAtlas incident library documents real outages where these practices would have changed the outcome.
sections.summary: Reliability is a target you choose, pay for, and verify, not a property you hope for.

relations.note: Targets come before architecture.
SLOs are the measurement core of reliability engineering.

title: Does Your Business Need Five Nines?
description: Choosing an availability target from business impact, and understanding what each extra nine costs.
question: What availability target do we actually need?
aliases: how should I design for high availability
problems: how should I design for high availability
how much reliability engineering do we need

sections.overview: Availability targets translate into allowed downtime: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours per year, 99.99% about 53 minutes, and 99.999% about 5.3 minutes. Each extra nine typically requires a different architecture and operating model.
sections.context: Your system's availability is bounded by its dependencies. A service depending on five components at 99.95% each cannot honestly promise 99.99% without redundancy.
assumptions: You can estimate revenue or trust lost per hour of downtime.
Targets apply to user journeys, not individual servers.
whenToUse: Three nines: most internal tools and early products; single region, multi-zone.
Four nines: core revenue paths of established products; automated failover, careful change management, strong observability.
Five nines: payments, telecom, safety-critical systems; multi-region active-active, cell-based design, dedicated reliability teams.
whenNotToUse: Do not set five nines because it sounds right; with only about 5 minutes per year, any human-in-the-loop recovery already breaks it.
Do not promise an SLA stricter than your dependencies' SLAs allow.
sections.cost: Cost rises steeply per nine: redundant capacity, multi-region data replication, more rigorous release processes, and on-call staffing.
sections.organization: Higher targets require mature incident response, change management and on-call. Organizational capability is often the limiting factor.
failureModes: Single points of failure hidden in shared dependencies (DNS, identity, config).
Over-investment: complex multi-region systems that fail in new ways more often than the simple design did.
sections.summary: Set the target from business impact. Most products need three to four nines on critical journeys and less elsewhere.

chooseWhen: Downtime causes severe financial, legal or safety harm
avoidWhen: Human-driven recovery is part of the plan

relations.note: Higher targets need multi-site strategies.
Availability targets go together with recovery objectives.
SLOs express the chosen target.
Each nine requires removing another class of single points of failure.
The target should come from cost of downtime versus cost of prevention.

title: Active-Active vs Active-Passive
description: Multi-site strategies: serve from all sites at once, or keep standby sites (warm standby, pilot light) ready to take over.
question: Should our second site serve traffic all the time, or stand by for failover?

sources.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud (AWS Well-Architected)

sections.overview: Active-active runs production in multiple sites simultaneously, each serving traffic. Active-passive keeps a secondary site that takes over on failure, ranging from pilot light (minimal core running) to warm standby (scaled-down full stack).
sections.context: The deciding factors are RTO, RPO, data replication model and cost. Active-active demands that data be writable or partitioned across sites; active-passive demands reliable, rehearsed failover.
whenToUse: Active-active: near-zero RTO, global latency needs, and data that can be partitioned or replicated with acceptable consistency.
Active-passive: RTO of minutes to hours is acceptable; simpler data model with a single write primary.
whenNotToUse: Active-active with a single-primary database (writes still have one home).
Active-passive with failover that has never been tested.
sections.cost: Active-active pays for full capacity in all sites. Pilot light pays for data replication and minimal infrastructure; warm standby sits between.
failureModes: Failover never rehearsed and failing when needed.
Thundering herd on the surviving site when traffic shifts.
Cross-region dependencies that fail with the primary region.
sections.summary: Choose from RTO/RPO and data model. Rehearse failover regardless of the strategy.

values: RTO tens of minutes to hours

relations.note: Recovery objectives choose the strategy.
Removes the region as a single point of failure.
Shifting all traffic to one site at once.
Failover must be exercised to be trusted.

title: RTO and RPO
description: Recovery Time Objective (how long you can be down) and Recovery Point Objective (how much data you can lose).

sections.overview: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption. RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time since the last recoverable state.
application: RPO drives backup frequency and replication mode (asynchronous replication means RPO > 0).
RTO drives standby strategy and automation.
Set both per system, based on business impact.
examples: Nightly backups give an RPO up to 24 hours.
Synchronous replication can approach RPO zero at a latency cost.
sections.limitations: Objectives are meaningless without restore tests. An untested backup has unknown RTO and RPO.
sections.summary: Agree RTO and RPO with the business, then design and test recovery to meet them.

relations.note: Objectives select the DR strategy.

title: Circuit Breaker
description: Stops calling a failing dependency for a while so callers fail fast and the dependency can recover.

sections.overview: A circuit breaker tracks failures of calls to a dependency. After a threshold it opens and rejects calls immediately; after a cool-down it lets trial calls through (half-open) and closes again on success.
whenToUse: Every synchronous call to a dependency that can fail or slow down.
whenNotToUse: As a replacement for timeouts; breakers need timeouts to detect slowness.
implementation: Combine with timeouts, bulkheads and fallbacks.
sections.summary: Fail fast to protect both caller and dependency.

relations.note: Stops a failing dependency from exhausting callers.
Stops retries against a dependency known to be failing.

title: Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
description: Retrying transient failures with increasing, randomized delays and a cap on attempts.

sources.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

sections.overview: Retries hide transient failures. Exponential backoff spaces attempts further apart; jitter randomizes them so clients do not retry in sync.
whenToUse: Idempotent operations with transient failures.
whenNotToUse: Non-idempotent operations without idempotency keys.
At every layer of a deep call chain (retries multiply).
implementation: Use retry budgets or token buckets.
sections.summary: Retry rarely, with backoff and jitter, at a single layer.

relations.note: Backoff, jitter and budgets keep retries from multiplying load.
Usually deployed together.

title: Chaos Engineering
description: Running controlled experiments that inject failures to verify a system behaves as expected under stress.

sections.overview: Chaos engineering forms a hypothesis about steady-state behaviour, injects a realistic fault (instance loss, latency, dependency failure), and checks whether the hypothesis holds, with a controlled blast radius.
whenToUse: After basic observability and resilience patterns are in place.
Before relying on failover in production.
whenNotToUse: Without monitoring that can detect impact, or without a way to stop the experiment.
sections.summary: Find weaknesses deliberately before they find you.

relations.note: Experiments are useless if you cannot see their effect.
The best-known public example.
Experiments reveal hidden single points of failure.

title: Observability
description: The ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs: metrics, logs and traces.
problems: I can't tell why requests are slow

sections.overview: Monitoring tells you whether known things are wrong. Observability lets you ask new questions about behaviour you did not predict. It is built from correlated telemetry: metrics for trends, logs for events, traces for request paths.
sections.context: In distributed systems a single request touches many processes. Without correlated telemetry, debugging becomes guesswork. Observability is a prerequisite for microservices, Kubernetes and chaos engineering.
whenToUse: Any production system; the depth scales with system complexity.
whenNotToUse: Avoid collecting everything at full fidelity; observability cost can rival compute cost.
sections.cost: Ingest and retention pricing grow with traffic and cardinality. Sampling, aggregation and retention tiers keep cost in check.
implementation: Propagate trace context across every hop.
Alert on SLO burn rates rather than raw resource thresholds.
sections.summary: Invest in correlated telemetry before distributing the system.

relations.note: OpenTelemetry is the standard way to produce the telemetry observability depends on.
The three signal types compared.
SLOs turn telemetry into decisions.
You cannot manage reliability you cannot measure.

title: Distributed Tracing
description: Following a single request across services as a tree of timed spans.

sections.overview: Each service records spans (named, timed operations) tagged with a shared trace ID passed along in request headers. A tracing backend assembles spans into a trace showing where time went and where errors occurred.
sections.context: Tracing helps engineers understand request flows across services and is the main tool for latency debugging in microservices.
whenToUse: Any system with more than a couple of services on a request path.
Asynchronous flows, by propagating context through messages.
whenNotToUse: Tracing every request at full fidelity at high volume; use sampling.
failureModes: Sampling that drops exactly the slow or failed requests (consider tail-based sampling).
sections.summary: The microscope for distributed request paths.

relations.note: With requests visible end to end, reliability engineering gives the practices to manage the system you can now see.
An open-source tracing backend.
Shows which dependency is slowing everything down.

title: Metrics vs Logs vs Traces
description: What each telemetry signal is good for, what it costs, and how to use them together.
question: Which telemetry signals should we invest in first?

sections.overview: Metrics are numeric time series, cheap to store and ideal for alerting and trends. Logs are discrete event records, rich but expensive at volume. Traces are request-scoped trees of spans that explain latency and dependencies.
whenToUse: Metrics for SLOs, dashboards and alerts.
Logs for detailed context and audit.
Traces for cross-service latency and error attribution.
whenNotToUse: High-cardinality labels on metrics.
Logging every request body at volume.
Unsampled traces at very high throughput.
sections.summary: Alert on metrics, investigate with traces, confirm with logs, and link them with shared IDs.

values: Low per signal; cardinality drives cost

relations.note: Traces as one of the three signals.
A metrics system.

title: Prometheus vs Datadog
description: Self-hosted open-source monitoring compared with an integrated commercial observability platform.
question: Should we run Prometheus ourselves or pay for Datadog?

sections.overview: Prometheus is an open-source metrics system with a pull model and PromQL, usually paired with Grafana and long-term storage. Datadog is a SaaS platform covering metrics, logs, traces, APM and more.
whenToUse: Prometheus: Kubernetes-centric stacks, cost sensitivity at scale, teams able to run it.
Datadog: small teams wanting breadth quickly, mixed environments, little appetite for running monitoring.
whenNotToUse: Prometheus alone for logs and traces.
Datadog without cost governance; custom metrics and log volume can grow bills quickly.
sections.cost: Prometheus costs staff time and storage. Datadog costs scale with hosts, custom metrics and ingest. Compare at your projected volume.
sections.summary: Buy for breadth and speed; build on open source when scale makes the bill or lock-in unacceptable.

relations.note: Open-source option.
Commercial option.
An observability build vs buy decision.

title: OpenTelemetry
description: A vendor-neutral standard and toolkit for generating and exporting traces, metrics and logs.

sections.overview: OpenTelemetry provides APIs, SDKs, auto-instrumentation and the Collector for producing telemetry and sending it to any compatible backend.
sections.context: It decouples instrumentation from vendors: instrument once, then route to Jaeger, Prometheus, Datadog or others through the Collector.
whenToUse: New instrumentation in any language.
Avoiding lock-in to an observability vendor.
whenNotToUse: Maturity varies by language and signal; check status for your stack.
sections.summary: The default way to instrument services today.

relations.note: OpenTelemetry generates the spans and propagates the context that distributed tracing needs.
Exports traces to Jaeger.
Exports metrics to Prometheus.
Datadog accepts OTLP data.

title: Prometheus
description: An open-source metrics monitoring and alerting system with a pull model and the PromQL query language.

sections.overview: Prometheus scrapes metrics endpoints, stores time series locally, evaluates alert rules and sends alerts through Alertmanager.
whenToUse: Kubernetes and cloud-native metrics.
whenNotToUse: Long-term, global storage needs add-ons (Thanos, Mimir, Cortex).
High-cardinality labels degrade performance.

relations.note: Overlap in metrics and alerting.

title: Datadog
description: A SaaS observability platform for infrastructure metrics, APM, logs, traces and security.

sections.overview: Datadog collects telemetry through agents and integrations and provides unified dashboards, alerting and APM.
whenToUse: Fast, broad observability without running backends.
whenNotToUse: Unmanaged usage leads to large bills; set budgets and tag ownership.
sections.summary: Breadth and speed at a usage-based price.

relations.note: Includes an APM and tracing backend.

title: Jaeger
description: An open-source distributed tracing backend originally built at Uber.

sections.overview: Jaeger stores and visualizes traces, supports OpenTelemetry ingestion, and offers dependency graphs and trace comparison.
whenToUse: Self-hosted tracing.
whenNotToUse: Requires a storage backend sized for trace volume.

relations.note: Stores and displays traces.

title: SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
description: Measuring reliability from the user's perspective and using the allowed unreliability to make release decisions.

sections.overview: An SLI is a measured indicator (e.g. fraction of requests under 300 ms). An SLO is a target for it (99.9% over 28 days). The error budget is the allowed shortfall (0.1%). An SLA is a contractual promise, usually looser than the SLO.
application: When the budget is healthy, ship faster; when it is burning, prioritize reliability work.
Alert on burn rate instead of raw thresholds.
sections.limitations: SLOs measured at the wrong place (server instead of user experience) give false confidence.
sections.summary: Make reliability a number that drives decisions.

relations.note: Burn-rate alerts surface degradations before they cascade.
